findings.title: Balance sliding flag strongly depresses layoff survival
findings.statement: Accounts flagged for balance_sliding (n=493) have a six-month layoff survival rate of 34.7%, 33.5 percentage points lower than accounts without the flag (68.2%, n=4007).
findings.evidence: compare_flag tool on flag 'balance_sliding' showing n=493 with survival 34.7% vs n=4007 without survival 68.2%.
findings.caveat: Accounts with balance_sliding also have lower median cash buffers (13,748 vs 24,223) and higher spending ratios (0.997 vs 0.910), which contributes to their lower survival.

findings.title: Declining balance trend reduces six-month layoff survival by 25 percentage points
findings.statement: Accounts in the lowest quartile of monthly balance trend (balance_trend_pm from -23 to -0.004, n=1125) have a six-month layoff survival rate of 47.3%, compared to 72.5% for accounts in the third quartile (n=1125).
findings.evidence: survival_by_quantile tool on 'balance_trend_pm' with 4 bins showing survival rates from 47.3% (Q1, n=1125) to 72.5% (Q3, n=1125).
findings.caveat: Balance trends are correlated with overall buffer levels and net cash flow direction.

findings.title: Fee bleed flag correlates with counterintuitively higher layoff survival
findings.statement: Accounts flagged for fee_bleed (n=310) achieve a six-month layoff survival rate of 96.8%, compared to 62.1% for non-fee-bleed accounts (n=4190), representing a 34.7 percentage point increase.
findings.evidence: compare_flag tool for 'fee_bleed' showing n=310 with 96.8% layoff survival vs n=4190 without at 62.1% survival.
findings.caveat: Fee bleed accounts have much lower median spending ratios (0.658 vs 0.930) and spending amounts, giving them larger income cushions relative to expenses despite high relative fees.

findings.title: Higher number of standing orders reduces layoff survival
findings.statement: Accounts with 2 to 5 standing orders (n=706) have a six-month layoff survival rate of 48.0%, compared to 69.7% for accounts with 0 to 1 standing orders (n=2845), a 21.7 percentage point drop.
findings.evidence: survival_by_quantile tool on 'n_standing_orders' with 3 distinct quantile bins showing 69.7% layoff survival for 0-1 standing orders (n=2845) versus 48.0% for 2-5 standing orders (n=706).
findings.caveat: Accounts with more standing orders may have higher baseline fixed commitments, reducing overall spending flexibility.

findings.title: Income volatility sharply reduces layoff survival for moderate-spending households
findings.statement: For households in the middle spending-ratio tier (0.821 to 0.976), high income volatility (income_cv > 0.314, n=411) reduces six-month layoff survival to 56.4%, compared to 79.7% for low income volatility (income_cv <= 0.208, n=360), a 23.3 percentage point drop.
findings.evidence: crosstab_survival tool for spending_ratio by income_cv (bins=3) showing for spending_ratio 0.821-0.976, low income_cv (0.003-0.208, n=360) has 79.7% survival while high income_cv (0.314-3.21, n=411) drops to 56.4%.
findings.caveat: High income volatility accounts may have variable bonus months or seasonal income that affect buffer accumulation differently depending on baseline surplus.

findings.title: High household bills share of outflow correlates with greater layoff survival
findings.statement: Accounts in the top tier of household bills share (bills_share from 0.404 to 0.894, n=1125) achieve an 86.7% six-month layoff survival rate, compared to 56.2% for accounts with bills share below 0.199 (n=2250), a 30.5 percentage point advantage.
findings.evidence: survival_by_quantile tool on 'bills_share' showing 86.7% layoff survival for the top bin (0.404 to 0.894, n=1125) versus 56.2% for the bottom bin (0 to 0.199, n=2250).
findings.caveat: Accounts with a high bills share have a lower overall spending ratio (Spearman rho = -0.242), indicating that higher fixed bill proportions coincide with larger income surpluses.

findings.title: Cash economy flag reduces layoff survival despite higher nominal inflows
findings.statement: Accounts flagged for cash_economy (n=1022) have a six-month layoff survival rate of 50.2%, 18.5 percentage points lower than non-cash economy accounts (68.7%, n=3478).
findings.evidence: compare_flag tool for 'cash_economy' flag showing n=1022 accounts with 50.2% layoff survival versus n=3478 without at 68.7% survival.
findings.caveat: Cash economy accounts have higher median inflow (11,079 vs 7,038) but also higher median spending ratios (0.975 vs 0.908), leaving less margin when income drops.

findings.title: Loan stress severely degrades household layoff survival
findings.statement: Accounts flagged for loan_stress (n=103) achieve a six-month layoff survival rate of only 28.2%, compared to 65.4% for accounts without loan stress (n=4397), a 37.2 percentage point deficit.
findings.evidence: compare_flag tool for 'loan_stress' flag showing n=103 with 28.2% layoff survival versus n=4397 without at 65.4%.
findings.caveat: Accounts under loan stress have higher median spending ratios (1.009 vs 0.916), reflecting fixed debt burdens that cannot be easily scaled down during income shocks.

summary: Beyond liquid cash reserves, fixed commitments like standing orders and loan obligations substantially diminish household survival during income shocks. Income volatility sharply reduces six-month layoff survival for households operating at moderate spending levels, whereas a steady balance trend strongly protects resilience. Automated signals such as balance sliding, cash economy reliance, and heavy loan stress identify vulnerable accounts before buffers are fully depleted.
best_finding: Income volatility sharply reduces layoff survival for moderate-spending households

baseline_findings.caveat: Quartile spread; not adjusted for income.
